title: Data-Driven Performance Modeling and Inverter-Level Fault Screening of Two Utility-Scale PV Plants Using Generation and Weather Sensor Data
content: Reliable estimation of photovoltaic (PV) power from on-site weather measurements underpins both short-term forecasting and performance monitoring. This paper analyzes a public dataset containing 34 days of 15-minute inverter-level generation records and weather sensor measurements from two utility-scale PV plants in India, each with 22 inverters. We first characterize data quality, identifying incomplete timestamps and a tenfold scaling inconsistency in the DC power channel of one plant. We then benchmark a physics-based temperature-corrected model against multiple linear regression, random forest, gradient boosting, and a multilayer perceptron for estimating per-inverter AC power, using a strictly chronological train/test split. For Plant 1, all models achieve R2 > 0.988, with gradient boosting obtaining the lowest error (RMSE of 30.9 kW, 2.3% of peak), and the fitted temperature coefficient (−0.44%/°C) agrees with typical crystalline-silicon values. For Plant 2, weather-only models reach only R2 ≈ 0.77. A median-referenced inverter performance index and an availability analysis show that this gap is caused by inverter-side losses rather than model deficiency: Plant 2 exhibits 83.8% availability under irradiation above 0.3 kW/m2 and an estimated 21.6% energy loss in those periods, compared with 99.7% and 0.35% for Plant 1. The results demonstrate that simple, interpretable models combined with fleet-relative indices can separate weather-driven variability from equipment underperformance using only standard SCADA data.
